sections.title: How hyperscalers buy construction: the invisible market
ps: The biggest data-center awards are almost never competitively bid in public — hyperscalers run private frameworks with a short list of trusted GCs, negotiate directly, and wrap everything in NDAs; projects carry code names ('Mustang', 'Cowboy') even in government filings

Repeat relationships dominate: a builder proving itself on one campus gets the next negotiated award without a bid — which is why repeat-client percentage is a more telling metric for these firms than win rate

The consequence for outsiders: public market-share tracking systematically undercounts NDA-heavy builders — a contractor can grow billions in revenue with zero press releases, and its absence from announced project lists proves nothing
Permits, OSHA filings, utility interconnection requests, and local-government records are how analysts pierce the veil — the paper trail a physical gigawatt cannot avoid leaving

sections.title: Cooling choices: air, water, and the water-neutrality constraint
ps: Every watt a server consumes becomes heat that must leave the building; how you reject that heat is the biggest design fork in data centers — evaporative (water) cooling is more energy-efficient but consumes millions of gallons; dry (air) cooling spends more electricity to save water

Desert and drought-prone markets (Arizona, parts of Texas) increasingly demand 'water-neutral' or water-free designs — air-cooled chillers and closed-loop systems that sacrifice some power efficiency for social license to build

The metrics: PUE (power usage effectiveness — total facility power ÷ IT power; closer to 1.0 is better) and WUE (water usage effectiveness — liters per kWh of IT load); a design choice that improves one often worsens the other

AI racks are pushing liquid cooling inside the building (direct-to-chip, rear-door heat exchangers) — but that's a closed loop; the facility-level question of how heat finally leaves (wet vs dry) remains, and it's decided by geography and politics as much as engineering

sections.title: Hot aisles, cold aisles, and containment
ps: Server racks are arranged in alternating rows: cold aisles (where chilled air is supplied to equipment intakes) and hot aisles (where exhaust discharges) — preventing hot exhaust from mixing back into intakes is the fundamental airflow problem

Containment physically walls off one aisle type — doors, roof panels, blanking plates — so hot and cold air streams never mix; done well it cuts cooling energy dramatically and lets each rack run denser

It's built like interior construction: framed walls, ceilings, doors, and panels installed inside the data hall — which is why a GC can self-perform it as an in-house trade and control the data-hall fit-out critical path
Containment quality shows up in commissioning: leaky containment means recirculation, hot spots, and failed thermal tests — a fit-and-finish trade with mission-critical consequences

sections.title: Joint ventures: how mega-projects share risk and spread benefit
ps: On billion-dollar public projects, GCs routinely team as joint ventures — pooling bonding capacity, labor pools, and local knowledge while splitting risk in agreed shares; stadium and airport JVs of three or four firms are normal

Public owners often require or reward minority- and women-owned business (M/WBE) participation, so JV structures pair national CMs with certified local partners — both a policy goal and a genuine local-capacity channel
JV members are jointly responsible for delivery: one partner's failure lands on the others' bonds — so partner selection is as much underwriting as courtesy
Reading a JV name (four firms, one lead) tells you who holds the schedule pen (the lead CM), who brings political and community standing, and how the fee splits roughly follow scope shares

sections.title: Labor relations on the megasite: unions, open shop, and safety compacts
ps: US construction splits between union labor (hiring halls, negotiated wages/benefits, jurisdictional rules) and open-shop/merit-shop labor; most southern markets run open-shop, while big industrial projects in the Midwest and Northeast often run union or mixed

Federal labor law (the NLRA) makes refusing to hire workers because of union affiliation illegal — 'salting' cases, where union members apply openly and rejections get litigated, are a recurring data-center-site risk that lands on subcontractors and embarrasses everyone above them

OSHA Strategic Partnerships are voluntary compacts among a GC, OSHA, and unions on a specific mega-project: negotiated injury-rate targets (TCIR/DART below industry baselines), site-wide rules stricter than code (6-ft fall protection), certified supervisor training, and daily audits

TCIR (total case incident rate) and DART (days away/restricted/transferred) are injuries per 100 full-time workers per year — the two numbers by which sites, GCs, and their insurance pricing are judged

sections.title: Reading private-company numbers: why the rankings disagree
ps: Private contractors publish no audited financials — the revenue you see is self-reported to survey rankers (ENR, BD+C, Forbes), each with different definitions, fiscal cutoffs, and lag; the same firm can legitimately show $8.5B and $10.2B in the same year

ENR ranks by total construction revenue; BD+C ranks by sector revenue (its data-center list is the AI-era scoreboard); Forbes lists total company revenue on a lagged calendar — know which lens each number comes through
Sector rankings measure trailing revenue, not forward share: a builder can lose every new award for a year and still climb the list on work billed from old backlog — and vice versa
For NDA-heavy firms, triangulate: CEO statements (percent-of-projects figures), utility-board appointments, OSHA filings, and client-side disclosures often say more than the rankings do

flashcards.q: Why do the largest data-center construction awards rarely appear in public bid records?
flashcards.a: Hyperscalers negotiate directly with a short list of trusted GCs under NDAs, using code names even in government filings. Repeat relationships replace competitive bidding — so a builder's absence from announced project lists proves nothing about its actual pipeline.

flashcards.q: How can analysts track construction work that companies never announce?
flashcards.a: Through the paper trail a physical project can't avoid: building permits, OSHA filings and partnership agreements, utility interconnection requests, local zoning records, and client-side disclosures. A gigawatt of construction is invisible in press releases but not in public records.

flashcards.q: What is PUE and what does a value close to 1.0 mean?
flashcards.a: Power Usage Effectiveness = total facility power ÷ IT equipment power. A PUE of 1.2 means every watt of computing carries 0.2 watts of overhead (mostly cooling). Closer to 1.0 = more efficient facility; the metric drove a decade of cooling innovation.

flashcards.q: What is the core trade-off between evaporative (water) cooling and dry (air) cooling?
flashcards.a: Evaporating water rejects heat very efficiently but consumes millions of gallons annually. Dry cooling uses no water but spends more electricity moving air. Water-scarce markets increasingly force 'water-neutral' air-cooled designs — trading PUE for social license to build.

Water Usage Effectiveness: liters of water consumed per kWh of IT energy. The water-side sibling of PUE — and often in tension with it, since designs that improve energy efficiency (evaporative cooling) usually worsen water consumption.

flashcards.q: What problem does hot-aisle/cold-aisle containment solve?
flashcards.a: Preventing hot server exhaust from mixing back into equipment intakes. Racks face each other across cold aisles (chilled supply) and back onto hot aisles (exhaust); containment walls off one stream with doors, panels, and ceilings so the two never mix — cutting cooling energy and enabling denser racks.

flashcards.q: Why can a general contractor self-perform aisle containment, and why does it matter?
flashcards.a: Containment is essentially interior construction — framed walls, ceilings, doors, blanking panels — inside the data hall. Self-performing it gives the GC direct control of the data-hall fit-out critical path, and its quality shows up in commissioning: leaks mean recirculation, hot spots, and failed thermal tests.

flashcards.q: Why do contractors form joint ventures on billion-dollar projects?
flashcards.a: To pool bonding capacity, labor pools, and local knowledge while splitting delivery risk in agreed shares. Public owners also often require or reward certified minority/women-owned business participation, so national CMs pair with local certified partners. JV members are jointly liable — partner choice is underwriting.

flashcards.q: What are TCIR and DART rates?
flashcards.a: The two standard construction-safety metrics, both counted per 100 full-time workers per year: TCIR is total recordable injury cases; DART counts the serious subset causing days away, restriction, or transfer. Sites, GCs, and their insurance pricing are judged on both against BLS industry baselines.

flashcards.q: What is an OSHA Strategic Partnership?
flashcards.a: A voluntary compact among a GC, OSHA, and (often) unions for one specific mega-project: negotiated injury-rate targets below industry baselines, site rules stricter than code (e.g., fall protection at 6 ft), certified supervisor training, and daily audits — cooperative regulation instead of pure enforcement.

flashcards.q: What is 'salting' in construction labor law?
flashcards.a: Union members openly applying for jobs at non-union contractors; refusing to hire them because of union affiliation violates federal labor law (the NLRA). Salting cases are a recurring megasite risk — the violation lands on a subcontractor but embarrasses the GC and owner above it.

flashcards.q: Why can the same private contractor show two different revenue figures in the same year?
flashcards.a: Private firms self-report to survey rankers with different definitions, fiscal cutoffs, and lag: ENR counts construction revenue on its cycle, Forbes lists lagged total company revenue, BD+C slices by sector. Neither is audited — triangulate against CEO statements and client-side records.
